ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (agreement number: 2324-123).

As novelty processing has been robustly associated with eye movements (see Meister & Buffalo, 2015, for a review) and pupil dilation (Beukema et al., 2019; Chen & Westermann, 2018; Kafkas et al., 2021), participants completed three eye-tracking tasks designed to assess novelty processing: two adapted VPC tasks (previously validated by Servais & Bastin, 2026), one using objects and one using scenes, and a pupil-recording task.
table.formatted: As novelty processing has been robustly associated with eye movements (see Meister & Buffalo, 2015, for a review) and pupil dilation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Beukema et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Chen & Westermann, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kafkas et al., 2021)</ref>, participants completed three eye-tracking tasks designed to assess novelty processing: two adapted VPC tasks (previously validated by <ref type="bibr">Servais & Bastin, 2026)</ref>, one using objects and one using scenes, and a pupil-recording task.

table.text: Participants were recruited using the existing GDPR-compliant volunteer database at GIGA-CRC Human Imaging and through advertisements on social media.
Two participants were lefthanded, one was ambidextrous, and the remaining participants were right-handed.
After being informed of the study procedures and providing written informed consent, participants completed two experimental sessions lasting approximately 75 and 90 minutes, respectively.
During the second session, participants completed a series of cognitive tasks.
During the experiment, participants were presented with 30 stimuli per condition (Absolute novelty, Associative novelty, and Familiar) that were presented in a random order.
Participants were instructed to keep their gaze fixed at the center of the screen and to remain still throughout the experiment.
To reduce eye fatigue, participants were given a short break after every nine images, during which they could blink or close their eyes.
Then, participants completed a forced-choice recognition task in which they were presented with pairs of images and asked to identify the previously seen image.

In our study, due to time constraints, we administered only Set 1 of the stimuli and assessed recognition after a 5-minute delay during which participants completed the items of the TCI-R questionnaire described below.

Finally, participants completed the items from the Temperament and Character Inventory-Revised (TCI-R; Hansenne et al., 2005) that assess the novelty-seeking trait, as this personality dimension could influence the propensity of participants to exhibit a novelty preference in the eye-tracking tasks (Krebs et al., 2009).
table.formatted: Finally, participants completed the items from the Temperament and Character Inventory-Revised (TCI-R; <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hansenne et al., 2005)</ref> that assess the novelty-seeking trait, as this personality dimension could influence the propensity of participants to exhibit a novelty preference in the eye-tracking tasks <ref type="bibr">(Krebs et al., 2009)</ref>.

table.text: In the object discrimination task, participants were presented with 48 triplets of images, each comprising two images depicting the same object from different viewpoints and a third image showing a different exemplar of the same object.
Participants were asked to identify the odd image.
In the study phase, participants were shown 30 images of objects presented one by one for 3 sec each, and they were asked to indicate whether the depicted object could fit in a shoebox or not.
Participants were instructed to memorize the items for a subsequent memory test.

After a two-minute retention interval filled with arithmetic exercises, participants completed the recognition phase, which was run using the Speed and Accuracy Boosting (SAB) procedure with a response deadline set at 750 ms from stimulus onset to recognize 30 old items from 30 new/distractor items.

Participants were asked to give a Go-response by pressing a key before the response deadline for the 'old' items they saw during the study phase, or a no-Go response for the "new/distractors items" that were not presented during the study phase.
Following encoding, participants completed a 30-s distractor task in which they counted backward from 100.
Participants were asked to select the name that had previously been associated with the face by pressing the left or right arrow key.
Participants were included in the analyses if at least 75% of their gaze samples were valid overall and if they contributed a minimum of 15 valid trials, out of 30, in each experimental condition.

Participants completed both part 1 and part 2 using different subsets, ensuring no overlap in stimuli across parts.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: This study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (agreement number: 2324-123). The sample size was estimated a priori by means of the G*Power 3.1 software (Faul et al., 2007). To detect a medium effect size correlation (r=.30) with a statistical power of .80 at α-threshold .05, the required sample size was at least 64 participants. Participants were recruited using the existing GDPR-compliant volunteer database at GIGA-CRC Human Imaging and through advertisements on social media. Exclusion criteria involve neurological or psychiatric history, and eye diseases (macula, glaucoma, cataract, etc.). We only recruited participants who were able to clearly see images on a screen without wearing glasses to avoid interference with the eye-tracker and ensure data quality.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps < .05", "p-values < .05", "p-values < .05", 
"ps > .56", "ps > .11", "ps > .08"), Text = c("Across fixation time, fixation count, and intra-AOI saccades, novelty preference remained significantly greater than zero in both Absolute and Associative conditions, and consistently larger for Associative than Absolute pairs (all ps < .05).", 
"In the Associative condition, novelty preference became significantly above 0 in the 100-200 ms bin and remained significant until the end of the trial (2500ms; all FDR-corrected p-values < .05).", 
"In the Absolute novelty condition, novelty preference first became significantly greater than 0 in the 500-600 ms bin and remained significantly above 0 through the end of the trial (all FDR-corrected p-values < .05).", 
"None of the stimulus-level covariates was significantly associated with peak dilation (all ps > .56).", 
"Neither the Associative novelty condition, b = 0.018, SE = 0.036, z =0.49, p = .624, nor the Absolute novelty condition, b = -0.008, SE = 0.035, z = -0.24, p = .812, differed significantly from the Familiar condition, and none of the stimulus-level covariates was significantly associated with peak dilation (all ps > .11).",

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. table.text: Welch's t-test revealed that average novelty rating was significantly higher in the incongruent object-in-scene images compared to the congruent object-in-scene images (t(346.47) = 4.29, p < .001, d = 0.45).

table.text: However, novelty was significantly less important for the incongruent object-in-scene images compared to the scene images from the Absolute (t(50.82) = -30.06, p < .001, d = -5.12) and Associative novelty (t(36.55) = -21.17, p < .001, d = -4.64) conditions after correcting p-values using Holm correction.

live_data_statements: As novelty processing has been robustly associated with eye movements (see Meister & Buffalo, 2015, for a review) and pupil dilation (Beukema et al., 2019; Chen & Westermann, 2018; Kafkas et al., 2021), participants completed three eye-tracking tasks designed to assess novelty processing: two adapted VPC tasks (previously validated by Servais & Bastin, 2026), one using objects and one using scenes, and a pupil-recording task.
Participants were recruited using the existing GDPR-compliant volunteer database at GIGA-CRC Human Imaging and through advertisements on social media.
We recruited 78 healthy Belgian participants.
Two participants were lefthanded, one was ambidextrous, and the remaining participants were right-handed.
After being informed of the study procedures and providing written informed consent, participants completed two experimental sessions lasting approximately 75 and 90 minutes, respectively.
During the second session, participants completed a series of cognitive tasks.
During the experiment, participants were presented with 30 stimuli per condition (Absolute novelty, Associative novelty, and Familiar) that were presented in a random order.
Participants were instructed to keep their gaze fixed at the center of the screen and to remain still throughout the experiment.
To reduce eye fatigue, participants were given a short break after every nine images, during which they could blink or close their eyes.
Then, participants completed a forced-choice recognition task in which they were presented with pairs of images and asked to identify the previously seen image.

In our study, due to time constraints, we administered only Set 1 of the stimuli and assessed recognition after a 5-minute delay during which participants completed the items of the TCI-R questionnaire described below.

Finally, participants completed the items from the Temperament and Character Inventory-Revised (TCI-R; Hansenne et al., 2005) that assess the novelty-seeking trait, as this personality dimension could influence the propensity of participants to exhibit a novelty preference in the eye-tracking tasks (Krebs et al., 2009).

In the object discrimination task, participants were presented with 48 triplets of images, each comprising two images depicting the same object from different viewpoints and a third image showing a different exemplar of the same object.
Participants were asked to identify the odd image.
In the study phase, participants were shown 30 images of objects presented one by one for 3 sec each, and they were asked to indicate whether the depicted object could fit in a shoebox or not.
Participants were instructed to memorize the items for a subsequent memory test.

After a two-minute retention interval filled with arithmetic exercises, participants completed the recognition phase, which was run using the Speed and Accuracy Boosting (SAB) procedure with a response deadline set at 750 ms from stimulus onset to recognize 30 old items from 30 new/distractor items.

Participants were asked to give a Go-response by pressing a key before the response deadline for the 'old' items they saw during the study phase, or a no-Go response for the "new/distractors items" that were not presented during the study phase.
Following encoding, participants completed a 30-s distractor task in which they counted backward from 100.
Participants were asked to select the name that had previously been associated with the face by pressing the left or right arrow key.
Participants were included in the analyses if at least 75% of their gaze samples were valid overall and if they contributed a minimum of 15 valid trials, out of 30, in each experimental condition.
Participants were recruited via Prolifics.

For each trial, both images were displayed simultaneously, and participants were asked to judge how likely it is for the object to appear in the given room.
Trials were randomized according to experimental conditions (congruent vs. incongruent pairings) to ensure variability in presentation order.
Participants completed both part 1 and part 2 using different subsets, ensuring no overlap in stimuli across parts.

info.title: Novelty Processing in Aging: Absence of an Association with Episodic Memory Abilities

author.affiliation:
GIGA Research

									Belgium

GIGA Research

									Belgium

text.text: Conceptually, novelty processing and episodic memory are closely linked.
Yet it remains unclear whether they rely on common or partly independent mechanisms.
We investigated whether their relationship depends on the type of novelty and representational content in healthy older adults.

Seventy-eight adults aged 61-84 years completed eye-tracking tasks assessing Absolute novelty (unknown stimuli) and Associative novelty (novel configurations of familiar elements) for objects and scenes, as well as a pupillometry task assessing responses to novel objects.
Novelty-processing indices were correlated with performance across various episodic memory tasks using preregistered Bayesian correlations.
Older adults showed reliable gaze preferences for both Absolute and Associative novelty in object and scene tasks.

Contrary to our predictions, however, Absolute novelty preference was generally unrelated to performance on familiarity-based recognition and perceptual discrimination measures hypothesized to rely on the perirhinal cortex.
Associative novelty preference was likewise largely unrelated to episodic memory performance, although a small number of unexpected associations with verbal recall emerged for object novelty.
Novelty-related pupil responses also showed little evidence of associations with memory performance.

Exploratory comparisons with data from younger adults aged 18-30 years (from Servais & Bastin, 2026)    indicated largely comparable gaze-based novelty preferences across age groups, although novelty-related peak pupil dilation was reduced in older adults.
text.formatted: Exploratory comparisons with data from younger adults aged 18-30 years (from Servais & Bastin, 2026)    indicated largely comparable gaze-based novelty preferences across age groups, although novelty-related peak pupil dilation was reduced in older adults.

text.text: Overall, these findings suggest that individual differences in novelty processing, when assessed in paradigms with no memory confound, are largely independent of episodic memory performance in healthy older adults and that gaze-based novelty processing may remain preserved with age for both novelty types.
Novelty detection, a fundamental property of human behavior, is conceptually associated with the cognitive function of episodic memory.
Indeed, memorizing new information relies on distinguishing the new from the familiar (van Kesteren et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Indeed, memorizing new information relies on distinguishing the new from the familiar <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(van Kesteren et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: While the link between the two processes seems obvious, its exact nature remains unclearare they two sides of the same function or rather distinct yet interacting mechanisms?
Surprisingly, consensus is lacking on whether novelty processing is a separate function or pertains to episodic memory.
Several cognitive models make different predictions.

Unitary models treat novelty as part of the memory system on a continuum with familiarity (Brown et al., 2002; Kumaran et al., 2007), whilst modular models (Kafkas et al., 2014) propose that information processing starts within two independent modules: one dealing with novelty and the other with familiarity.
text.formatted: Unitary models treat novelty as part of the memory system on a continuum with familiarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Brown et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Kumaran et al., 2007)</ref>, whilst modular models <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kafkas et al., 2014)</ref> propose that information processing starts within two independent modules: one dealing with novelty and the other with familiarity.

text.text: The two signals then interact to produce a signal of relative familiarity.
Critically, we suggest considering the distinction between different types of novelty to investigate their relationships with memory.

Absolute novelty (stimulus never met) is commonly distinguished from Associative novelty (new configuration of otherwise familiar stimuli) or contextual novelty (familiar item encountered in unexpected context) (Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018; Schomaker et al., 2015), and we suggest that these different novelty types could entertain different relationships with memory (Bastin et al., 2019; Servais et al., 2024; Servais & Bastin, 2024).
text.formatted: Absolute novelty (stimulus never met) is commonly distinguished from Associative novelty (new configuration of otherwise familiar stimuli) or contextual novelty (familiar item encountered in unexpected context) <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Schomaker et al., 2015)</ref>, and we suggest that these different novelty types could entertain different relationships with memory <ref type="bibr">(Bastin et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Servais et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Servais & Bastin, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, while it is well acknowledged that novelty processing and episodic memory both rely on the medial temporal lobe (MTL) brain regions (Schomaker et al., 2021; Tulving et al., 1994), Kafkas & Montaldi (2018) recently suggested separate brain circuits that process novelty differently depending on its nature.
text.formatted: Indeed, while it is well acknowledged that novelty processing and episodic memory both rely on the medial temporal lobe (MTL) brain regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Schomaker et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Tulving et al., 1994)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kafkas & Montaldi (2018)</ref> recently suggested separate brain circuits that process novelty differently depending on its nature.

text.text: On one hand, Absolute novelty could be processed as an absence of familiarity by the perirhinal cortex (PRC)-linking it to the cholinergic system (Okada et al., 2022; Warburton et al., 2003).
text.formatted: On one hand, Absolute novelty could be processed as an absence of familiarity by the perirhinal cortex (PRC)-linking it to the cholinergic system <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Okada et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Warburton et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Defining novelty in relation to prior knowledge aligns with recent accounts of the PRC, which emphasize its representational role beyond memory (Bastin & Delhaye, 2023).

text.text: In this view, the PRC is thought to support high-level object representations and the processing of complex objects, feature conjunctions, and familiarity independently of explicit recognition memory (Cowell et al., 2019; Ladyka-Wojcik et al., 2026; Martin & Barense, 2023; Ranganath & Ritchey, 2012).

text.text: On the other hand, Associative and contextual novelty could activate the hippocampus, triggering functional loops that connect it to dopaminergic nuclei (Clos et al., 2019) including the ventral tegmental area (VTA), and to noradrenergic nucleus including the locus coeruleus (LC; Groves et al., 2025; McNamara & Dupret, 2017; Park, 2024; Schneider et al., 2024).

text.text: Furthermore, novelty-and memory-related electrophysiological signals differ within the hippocampus, probably generated by different neuronal populations, allowing it to couple with two mutually exclusive networks and brain states (novelty processing vs remembering, Barbeau et al., 2017).

text.text: Several experimental paradigms have been traditionally used to assess novelty processing, including oddball tasks, repetition-suppression designs, visual paired comparison (VPC) paradigms, old/new recognition tasks, and Associative novelty paradigms.

However, many of these paradigms rely on a familiarization phase or on prior exposure within the laboratory to establish a contrast between familiar and novel stimuli, thereby making memory a key component of the task.

In repetition-suppression paradigms, for instance, novelty is inferred from stronger neural responses to non-repeated than repeated stimuli (Barto et al., 2013; Nyberg, 2005; Ranganath & Rainer, 2003; Reichardt et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In repetition-suppression paradigms, for instance, novelty is inferred from stronger neural responses to non-repeated than repeated stimuli <ref type="bibr">(Barto et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nyberg, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ranganath & Rainer, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Reichardt et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, in oddball paradigms, infrequent deviant stimuli are interspersed among frequently presented standard stimuli, with enhanced behavioral or neural responses to the deviants taken as evidence of novelty detection (Friedman et al., 2001; Polich, 2007).
text.formatted: Similarly, in oddball paradigms, infrequent deviant stimuli are interspersed among frequently presented standard stimuli, with enhanced behavioral or neural responses to the deviants taken as evidence of novelty detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Friedman et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Polich, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Old/new recognition tasks require participants to discriminate newly presented stimuli from items previously encountered during an encoding phase, thereby making novelty judgments dependent on prior episodic exposure (Ranganath & Rainer, 2003).
text.formatted: Old/new recognition tasks require participants to discriminate newly presented stimuli from items previously encountered during an encoding phase, thereby making novelty judgments dependent on prior episodic exposure <ref type="bibr">(Ranganath & Rainer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Associative novelty paradigms also usually require participants to first learn specific item-item, item-context, or item-location associations, after which novelty is defined as the violation, rearrangement, or recombination of these recently learned associations (Kumaran & Maguire, 2007; Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018).
text.formatted: Associative novelty paradigms also usually require participants to first learn specific item-item, item-context, or item-location associations, after which novelty is defined as the violation, rearrangement, or recombination of these recently learned associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kumaran & Maguire, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, in VPC tasks, novelty preference is assessed after one stimulus has been familiarized, with longer looking times toward the novel stimulus typically interpreted as evidence of novelty detection (Allegretti et al., 2024; Boujelbane et al., 2024; Crutcher et al., 2009; Fagan, 1970; Manns et al., 2000; Meister & Buffalo, 2015).
text.formatted: Similarly, in VPC tasks, novelty preference is assessed after one stimulus has been familiarized, with longer looking times toward the novel stimulus typically interpreted as evidence of novelty detection <ref type="bibr">(Allegretti et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Boujelbane et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Crutcher et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fagan, 1970;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Manns et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Meister & Buffalo, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Although these approaches are highly informative, they make novelty processing difficult to disentangle from memory processes, because the "novel" response is defined relative to what has just been encoded, retained, or recognized.

For example, this critical confound has been well acknowledged for VPC tasks, which have long been used in preverbal infants and non-verbal populations as measures of implicit recognition memory (Basile et al., 2024; Eizenman et al., 2019; Fagan, 1970; Leeman-Markowski et al., 2024; Manns et al., 2000; Richmond et al., 2007).
text.formatted: For example, this critical confound has been well acknowledged for VPC tasks, which have long been used in preverbal infants and non-verbal populations as measures of implicit recognition memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Basile et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Eizenman et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fagan, 1970;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Leeman-Markowski et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Manns et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Richmond et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, such tasks may confound novelty processing with implicit memory, making them less suitable for examining the relationships between novelty processing and episodic memory.

The rarity of studies investigating novelty against prior knowledge is especially surprising given the rising interest in differentiating episodic familiarity (i.e., the sense of recognizing something based on a specific encounter) from lifetime familiarity (i.e., the gradual accumulation of familiarity with object concepts over the course of life) in the memory literature (Anderson et al., 2021; Bowles et al., 2016; Duke et al., 2017; Servais et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2023).

text.text: Despite this growing theoretical interest, experimental studies of novelty have rarely operationalized novelty specifically in relation to prior knowledge.

Although a small number of studies have examined Absolute novelty processing using unfamiliar non-objects (Harı & Demiralp, 2025), rare or uncommon objects (Blackford et al., 2010), or abstract fractals (Stoppel et al., 2009), and others have investigated what we refer to here as Associative novelty using familiar objects with unusual features (Michelon et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013), no study, to our knowledge, has systematically examined both Absolute and Associative novelty as a function of pre-existing prior knowledge.
text.formatted: Although a small number of studies have examined Absolute novelty processing using unfamiliar non-objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Harı & Demiralp, 2025)</ref>, rare or uncommon objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Blackford et al., 2010)</ref>, or abstract fractals <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Stoppel et al., 2009)</ref>, and others have investigated what we refer to here as Associative novelty using familiar objects with unusual features <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Michelon et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Wang et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Zhang et al., 2013)</ref>, no study, to our knowledge, has systematically examined both Absolute and Associative novelty as a function of pre-existing prior knowledge.

text.text: This distinction is important because novelty in everyday life is not always defined by recent exposure.
Rather, an object, entity, scene, or association can be novel because it is absent from an individual's long-term knowledge, or because familiar elements are combined in an unexpected way.

In addition to differences between types of novelty, novelty can also occur at different representational levels, such as objects or scenes (for example, Quent et al., 2021 distinguished the item from the context).

text.text: In parallel, recent representational accounts consider that the ventral visual stream and MTL form a continuous representational hierarchy, organized along a posterior-to-anterior gradient of increasing representational complexity (Graham et al., 2010; Saksida & Bussey, 2010).

text.text: According to this view, distinct brain regions of the MTL are involved in the processing of representations of different nature, rather than exclusively in terms of processes or operations (Martin & Barense, 2023).

text.text: Notably, substantial evidence supports the critical role of the PRC in object processing (Cowell et al., 2019; Martin & Barense, 2023; Ranganath & Ritchey, 2012), whereas the hippocampus is assumed to play a central role in scene processing (Dalton et al., 2018; Gardette et al., 2024).

text.text: This is particularly relevant for novelty processing because it contrasts with accounts suggesting that the PRC primarily supports the detection of Absolute novelty, whereas the hippocampus is more involved in Associative novelty processing (Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018).

text.text: Rather than mapping brain regions onto the processing of novelty types in a fixed manner, the representational account suggests that their contribution may further depend on the type of novel information.
The present study therefore investigates novelty processing across both object and scene representations.
This approach allows us to test whether the relationship between novelty processing and episodic memory depends on novelty types and representational content.
To this end, in the current study, we used the NOVITAS stimulus database we developed in Servais and Bastin (2026).
text.formatted: To this end, in the current study, we used the NOVITAS stimulus database we developed in <ref type="bibr">Servais and Bastin (2026)</ref>.

text.text: This database contains images of both objects and scenes representing two types of novelty: Absolute novelty and Associative novelty.

As novelty processing has been robustly associated with eye movements (see Meister & Buffalo, 2015, for a review) and pupil dilation (Beukema et al., 2019; Chen & Westermann, 2018; Kafkas et al., 2021), participants completed three eye-tracking tasks designed to assess novelty processing: two adapted VPC tasks (previously validated by Servais & Bastin, 2026), one using objects and one using scenes, and a pupil-recording task.
text.formatted: As novelty processing has been robustly associated with eye movements (see Meister & Buffalo, 2015, for a review) and pupil dilation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Beukema et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Chen & Westermann, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kafkas et al., 2021)</ref>, participants completed three eye-tracking tasks designed to assess novelty processing: two adapted VPC tasks (previously validated by <ref type="bibr">Servais & Bastin, 2026)</ref>, one using objects and one using scenes, and a pupil-recording task.

text.text: In the adapted VPC tasks, a familiar object or scene (i.e., a well-known common object or place) was presented alongside either an associatively novel stimulus (i.e., a novel object or scene created by recombining features of familiar objects or places) or an absolutely novel stimulus (i.e., an object or scene that has never been encountered before).
Novelty processing was assessed through fixation duration, fixation count, saccade count, and the proportion of trials in which the first fixation was directed toward the novel image.

Although these eye-movement measures have been widely used in classical VPC tasks (Meister & Buffalo, 2015), they have also been validated in these novel VPC adaptations that omit a familiarization phase (Servais & Bastin, 2026).

text.text: According to Kafkas et al. (2021), we would expect pupil constriction for Absolute novelty and pupil dilation for Associative novelty.

text.text: Our main goal was to investigate how different types of novelty relate to episodic memory.
Based on the literature described above, we hypothesized a unitary relation for Absolute novelty and relative independence for Associative novelty.

To investigate these relationships, we included memory tasks that are thought to rely predominantly on perirhinal cortex (PRC)-dependent processes, such as familiarity-based recognition, as well as tasks that rely more strongly on hippocampal processes, such as free recall and associative memory.

Specifically, if Absolute novelty relies on mechanisms that overlap with familiarity-based recognition, we expected individual differences in Absolute novelty processing to correlate with performance on tasks involving PRC-dependent processes, including the entity recognition task (Besson et al., 2020), the object and scene odd-one-out tasks (Delhaye et al., 2025), the Doors memory test (Baddeley et al., 1994), and the DMS48 recognition test (Barbeau et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Specifically, if Absolute novelty relies on mechanisms that overlap with familiarity-based recognition, we expected individual differences in Absolute novelty processing to correlate with performance on tasks involving PRC-dependent processes, including the entity recognition task <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Besson et al., 2020)</ref>, the object and scene odd-one-out tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Delhaye et al., 2025)</ref>, the Doors memory test <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baddeley et al., 1994)</ref>, and the DMS48 recognition test <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Barbeau et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, we expected weaker or no associations with tasks relying more strongly on hippocampal processes, such as the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test (Grober et al., 1987) and a face-name associative memory task (inspired by Macoir et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In contrast, we expected weaker or no associations with tasks relying more strongly on hippocampal processes, such as the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Grober et al., 1987)</ref> and a face-name associative memory task (inspired by <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Macoir et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For Associative novelty, if its detection relies on mechanisms that are relatively independent of those supporting episodic memory performance, we expected weak or no correlations with performance across all the selected memory tasks.
Regarding differences between objects and scenes, object-based Absolute novelty may be more closely linked to familiarity-based recognition and PRC representations.

In contrast, Associative novelty, and scene novelty more broadly, may rely more strongly on hippocampal representations and relational processing, without necessarily mapping directly onto episodic memory performance.
To answer our research question, main analyses examined correlations between episodic memory performance and the preference for different types of novelty.

The study was conducted in healthy adults over 60 years of age, as aging is associated with increased interindividual variability in memory performance, thereby providing a suitable context in which to examine individual differences in novelty processing and episodic memory.
The study was pre-registered at OSF (https://osf.io/zj8sq).

text.text: To detect a medium effect size correlation (r=.30) with a statistical power of .80 at α-threshold .05, the required sample size was at least 64 participants.
Participants were recruited using the existing GDPR-compliant volunteer database at GIGA-CRC Human Imaging and through advertisements on social media.
Exclusion criteria involve neurological or psychiatric history, and eye diseases (macula, glaucoma, cataract, etc.).
We only recruited participants who were able to clearly see images on a screen without wearing glasses to avoid interference with the eye-tracker and ensure data quality.
We recruited 78 healthy Belgian participants.

We excluded data from five participants for whom an intern assisting with data collection forgot to collect demographic information, one participant for whom eye-tracking calibration was unsuccessful due to droopy eyelids, and one participant who stopped before completing the study.
The sample considered at this stage therefore comprised 71 participants (52 females; 19 males) aged 61-84 years (M = 71.09 ± 6.37), with 8-24 years of education (M = 15.63 ± 3.22).
Two participants were lefthanded, one was ambidextrous, and the remaining participants were right-handed.
After being informed of the study procedures and providing written informed consent, participants completed two experimental sessions lasting approximately 75 and 90 minutes, respectively.
The average time interval between the two sessions was 7.28 days (min = 1 day and max = 43 days).
At the end of the experiment, all participants received financial compensation of 25 euros.

During the first session, participants first provided demographic information, including age, sex, and education level (defined as the number of successfully completed years of education since the first year of primary school).
They then completed three experimental eye-tracking tasks assessing novelty processing: an adapted VPC task with objects, an adapted VPC task with scenes, and a pupil recording task.
The order of these three eye-tracking tasks was randomized across participants.

The session continued with the following neuropsychological tests: the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA; Nasreddine & Patel, 2016), the DMS48 memory test (Set 1; Barbeau et al., 2004), and the items from the Temperament and Character Inventory-Revised (TCI-R, Hansenne et al., 2005) assessing the novelty-seeking personality trait.
text.formatted: The session continued with the following neuropsychological tests: the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA; Nasreddine & Patel, 2016), the DMS48 memory test (Set 1; <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Barbeau et al., 2004)</ref>, and the items from the Temperament and Character Inventory-Revised (TCI-R, <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hansenne et al., 2005)</ref> assessing the novelty-seeking personality trait.

text.text: During the second session, participants completed a series of cognitive tasks.

They first performed an entity recognition task, adapted and shortened from Besson et al. (2020), followed by the encoding and immediate free-and cued-recall phases of the French version of the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test (FCSRT; Grober et al., 1987).

text.text: Participants then completed odd-one-out tasks involving objects and scenes (based on Delhaye et al., 2025) and the Doors memory test (Baddeley et al., 1994).

text.text: After a 20-minute delay, they completed the delayed free-and cued-recall phases of the FCSRT.

The session concluded with a face-name associative memory task (adapted from the procedure described by Macoir et al., 2024), the Mill Hill Vocabulary Test (Deltour, 1998), and the Lexis 64 naming test (de Partz et al., 2001).

text.text: Details about each task are provided below.

The novelty detection tasks involved the two VPC-like tasks we previously validated for objects and for scenes (see Servais & Bastin, 2026), as well as a task measuring pupil diameter in response to novel images that we developed.

text.text: All these tasks were presented on a gray screen (hex colour # 808080) with a resolution of 1600 × 900 px.
OpenSesame 3.2.8 software (Mathôt et al., 2012) was used to control stimulus presentation.
text.formatted: OpenSesame 3.2.8 software <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mathôt et al., 2012)</ref> was used to control stimulus presentation.

text.text: Eye movements and pupil size were recorded at 500 Hz using the SMI Red 500 remote eye-tracker.
Synchronisation between stimulus presentation and eye-tracking recording was handled using the PyGaze plug-in implemented within the OpenSesame software (Dalmaijer et al., 2014).

text.text: The eye-tracker was positioned below the screen.
The eye-lens distance was 50-70 cm.
The tasks were administered in a room without windows to keep the room lighting conditions constant.
We used the two VPC-like tasks previously developed by Servais and Bastin (2026): one using object stimuli and one using scene stimuli.
text.formatted: We used the two VPC-like tasks previously developed by <ref type="bibr">Servais and Bastin (2026)</ref>: one using object stimuli and one using scene stimuli.

text.text: In both tasks, participants passively viewed pairs of images presented side by side while their eye movements were recorded.
They were instructed to view the images naturally, as if they were watching images on a television screen, and were explicitly informed that no memory test would follow.
This passive-viewing procedure was used to assess spontaneous visual preference for novel stimuli.
In the object VPC task, each trial presented two object images simultaneously.

The task included three conditions: a baseline condition, in which two images of the same familiar object were presented; an Associative novelty condition, in which an associatively novel object was shown next to a Familiar object; and an Absolute novelty condition, in which an absolutely novel object was shown next to a Familiar object.
Each image pair was preceded by a fixation cross of 500 ms and was displayed for 2.5 s.
One modification from Servais and Bastin (2026) was that object images in the present study were selected based on normative ratings obtained from older adults.
text.formatted: One modification from <ref type="bibr">Servais and Bastin (2026)</ref> was that object images in the present study were selected based on normative ratings obtained from older adults.

text.text: Specifically, objects with a mean novelty score above 75 were selected for the Associative and Absolute novelty conditions, whereas objects with a mean novelty score below 50 were selected as Familiar control stimuli.
The scene VPC task followed the same general procedure, but included four conditions: baseline, Associative novelty, Absolute novelty, and Incongruency.
In the Incongruency condition, participants viewed two versions of the same Familiar scene, one containing a congruent object and the other an incongruent object.
Scene pairs were displayed for 3.5 s.
The normative results for the congruent and incongruent object-in-scene images obtained from older adults are available in Supplementary Materials.

text.text: To maximize differences between experimental conditions in terms of novelty, we selected the 30 stimuli from the Associative novelty condition and the 30 stimuli from the Absolute novelty condition that obtained the highest average normative rating of novelty, and the 30 stimuli from the Familiar condition that obtained the lowest average normative rating of novelty (see Servais & Bastin, 2026 for the associated normative study in 184 older adults).

text.text: To avoid repeating stimuli across tasks, the stimuli that were selected for the pupil task were not included in the VPC tasks.

Because pupillary responses are sensitive to both light intensity (Cheng et al., 2006) and chromatic adaptation (Tsujimura et al., 2006), stimulus brightness, contrast, and the colour of visual images were controlled.

text.text: The experiment took place in a room without windows to avoid changes in ambient luminosity.
Following the method outlined by Kafkas and Montaldi (2015), we modified our images so that stimuli consisted of single objects presented in grayscale on a gray background (RGB = 130).

text.text: A consistent RGB value (red = 130, green = 130, blue = 130) was applied across all stimuli.
These modifications were made using the Pillow library from Python 3.0.
Additionally, the luminance of each image was verified by calculating the mean of pixel intensity using histograms from the GIMP software (version 2.10.38).
Stimuli with luminance values exceeding two standard deviations from the mean were further processed, and their luminance was reduced to 80%.
During the experiment, participants were presented with 30 stimuli per condition (Absolute novelty, Associative novelty, and Familiar) that were presented in a random order.
Each stimulus was presented at the center of the screen for 500 ms.

Central presentation (Kafkas & Montaldi, 2015) and brief exposure duration (Ruiz Chiapello et al., 2026) were used to minimize saccades during stimulus viewing, thereby helping to preserve the quality of the pupil data.

text.text: After each stimulus, a fixation cross was displayed at the center of the screen for 5500 ms.
This relatively long interval was chosen to allow the pupil signal to return to baseline before the next stimulus was presented (Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023; Ruiz Chiapello et al., 2026).

text.text: Before the task began, a 13-point calibration was performed to ensure the quality of the eye-tracking data.
Participants were instructed to keep their gaze fixed at the center of the screen and to remain still throughout the experiment.
To reduce eye fatigue, participants were given a short break after every nine images, during which they could blink or close their eyes.
They pressed a key when they were ready to continue. novelty processing.

We administered the French version of the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test (FCSRT, Grober et al., 2009), a widespread verbal episodic memory test that is known to rely on the hippocampus (Quenon et al., 2016; Sarazin et al., 2010).
text.formatted: We administered the French version of the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test <ref type="bibr">(FCSRT, Grober et al., 2009)</ref>, a widespread verbal episodic memory test that is known to rely on the hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Quenon et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Sarazin et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: For each of the three learning trials, we computed free recall, corresponding to the number of words recalled without cues, and total recall, corresponding to the sum of free and cued recall.
Free recall and total recall scores were then summed across the three learning trials.
We also calculated the Index of Sensitivity to Cueing (ISC), using the formula: ISC = (Total Recall -Free Recall) / (Total items -Free Recall).
These three indices have been shown to be sensitive to hippocampal function (Pelletier et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These three indices have been shown to be sensitive to hippocampal function <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Pelletier et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We also selected two tests of visual recognition that are presumably relying on the PRC.
First, we administered the DMS48 memory test (Barbeau et al., 2004).
text.formatted: First, we administered the DMS48 memory test <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Barbeau et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: This task was specifically designed to detect dysfunction in the MTL, particularly the PRC (Barbeau et al., 2004).
text.formatted: This task was specifically designed to detect dysfunction in the MTL, particularly the PRC <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Barbeau et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroimaging studies showed that anterior subhippocampal regions, including the PRC, were indeed involved in the DMS48 (Didic et al., 2010; Guedj et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Neuroimaging studies showed that anterior subhippocampal regions, including the PRC, were indeed involved in the DMS48 <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Didic et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Guedj et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: During the test, participants start with incidental encoding of the images during which they are shown a set of 48 images and asked whether there are more or fewer than three colours in each picture.
Then, participants completed a forced-choice recognition task in which they were presented with pairs of images and asked to identify the previously seen image.

In our study, due to time constraints, we administered only Set 1 of the stimuli and assessed recognition after a 5-minute delay during which participants completed the items of the TCI-R questionnaire described below.
We computed the total recognition score as the number of correctly recognized items out of 48.
Second, the Doors test (Baddeley et al., 1994) was included as an additional measure of visual forced-choice recognition memory.
text.formatted: Second, the Doors test <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baddeley et al., 1994)</ref> was included as an additional measure of visual forced-choice recognition memory.

text.text: Although the task is not specific to the PRC, patients with hippocampal damage can perform it successfully (Baddeley et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Although the task is not specific to the PRC, patients with hippocampal damage can perform it successfully <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baddeley et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, forced-choice recognition performance is thought to rely partly on familiarity-based processes, which have been linked to PRC functioning (Bastin & Van der Linden, 2003; Brown & Aggleton, 2001).
text.formatted: Moreover, forced-choice recognition performance is thought to rely partly on familiarity-based processes, which have been linked to PRC functioning <ref type="bibr">(Bastin & Van der Linden, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Brown & Aggleton, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: For each participant, we computed two scores: the number of doors correctly recognized in Parts A and B of the Doors test.

We analyzed the two subparts separately because Part A is generally considered to rely primarily on familiarity processes, whereas findings for Part B are mixed, suggesting that it may involve either familiarity or recollection depending on the strategy used by the participant to distinguish the target door from the three highly similar lures (see for example, Bastin et al., 2004).
text.formatted: We analyzed the two subparts separately because Part A is generally considered to rely primarily on familiarity processes, whereas findings for Part B are mixed, suggesting that it may involve either familiarity or recollection depending on the strategy used by the participant to distinguish the target door from the three highly similar lures (see for example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bastin et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Given that dual-process theories suggest that recollection is associated with hippocampal activity, whereas familiarity is more closely linked to perirhinal regions (Yonelinas & Jacoby, 2012), this distinction seems appropriate for our purpose.
text.formatted: Given that dual-process theories suggest that recollection is associated with hippocampal activity, whereas familiarity is more closely linked to perirhinal regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Yonelinas & Jacoby, 2012)</ref>, this distinction seems appropriate for our purpose.

text.text: To further characterize the participants in our sample, we administered the Montréal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA; Nasreddine & Patel, 2016) to ensure that they did not show significant cognitive decline, using a cut-off score of 23/30 (as advised in Carson et al., 2018).

text.text: Participants also completed the Mill Hill Vocabulary Test (Deltour, 1998), which was used as an index of socio-cultural level, and the Lexis 64 Naming Test (de Partz et al., 2001) to screen for substantial object-naming and lexico-semantic difficulties, as impaired processing or recognition of object stimuli could potentially affect novelty processing in our eye-tracking tasks.

text.text: Finally, participants completed the items from the Temperament and Character Inventory-Revised (TCI-R; Hansenne et al., 2005) that assess the novelty-seeking trait, as this personality dimension could influence the propensity of participants to exhibit a novelty preference in the eye-tracking tasks (Krebs et al., 2009).

text.text: We used the odd-one-out tasks for objects and scenes developed by Delhaye et al. (2025).
text.formatted: We used the odd-one-out tasks for objects and scenes developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Delhaye et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the object discrimination task, participants were presented with 48 triplets of images, each comprising two images depicting the same object from different viewpoints and a third image showing a different exemplar of the same object.
Participants were asked to identify the odd image.
The triplets were presented in a random order.
The scene task followed the same procedure.
For each task, we first computed overall accuracy as the number of correctly identified triplets.

Following Delhaye et al. (2025), we also computed an index of sensitivity to visual distance, as this measure was shown to relate specifically to the structural integrity of the transentorhinal cortex, a region encompassing the medial portion of the PRC.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Delhaye et al. (2025)</ref>, we also computed an index of sensitivity to visual distance, as this measure was shown to relate specifically to the structural integrity of the transentorhinal cortex, a region encompassing the medial portion of the PRC.

text.text: For each participant, this index was calculated as the point-biserial correlation between trial-by-trial accuracy and each trial's visual-distance index.
The resulting r values were then Fisher-transformed into Z scores.
Higher Z scores indicate that performance was more strongly affected by visual distance, with better accuracy for more visually distinct trials.
We used a shorter version of the recognition task for entities developed by Besson et al. (2020).
text.formatted: We used a shorter version of the recognition task for entities developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Besson et al. (2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the study phase, participants were shown 30 images of objects presented one by one for 3 sec each, and they were asked to indicate whether the depicted object could fit in a shoebox or not.
Participants were instructed to memorize the items for a subsequent memory test.

After a two-minute retention interval filled with arithmetic exercises, participants completed the recognition phase, which was run using the Speed and Accuracy Boosting (SAB) procedure with a response deadline set at 750 ms from stimulus onset to recognize 30 old items from 30 new/distractor items.
The SAB is based on a Go/no-Go task.

Participants were asked to give a Go-response by pressing a key before the response deadline for the 'old' items they saw during the study phase, or a no-Go response for the "new/distractors items" that were not presented during the study phase.
Feedback was provided after each trial to inform the participant about the correctness of their responses.
Before starting the task, participants performed a training block to get familiar with the procedure and speed.
Responses were classified according to both the stimulus type and the participant's response within the 750-ms deadline.
A hit corresponded to a Go response to an old item, whereas a false alarm corresponded to a Go response to a new/distractor item.

When no-Go response was given before the deadline, the trial was considered a no-Go response: this was classified as an omission when the stimulus was an old item, and as a correct rejection when the stimulus was a new/distractor item.

For each participant, recognition sensitivity was then quantified using d′, calculated by subtracting the z-transformed false alarm rate from the ztransformed hit rate: d′ = z(hit rate) -z(false alarm rate).
Higher d′ values indicate better discrimination between old and new items, independently of response bias.
The entity recognition task was selected because it has been shown to be associated with the integrity of the perirhinal and anterolateral entorhinal cortices (Besson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The entity recognition task was selected because it has been shown to be associated with the integrity of the perirhinal and anterolateral entorhinal cortices <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Besson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Participants performed a computerized face-name association memory task (inspired by the procedure from Macoir et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Participants performed a computerized face-name association memory task (inspired by the procedure from <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Macoir et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the encoding phase, they were presented with 32 face-name pairs and were instructed to memorize the association between each face and its corresponding first name.
The stimulus set included an equal number of male and female faces, as well as an equal number of young and older faces, selected from the database published by Minear and Park (2004).
text.formatted: The stimulus set included an equal number of male and female faces, as well as an equal number of young and older faces, selected from the database published by <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Minear and Park (2004)</ref>.

text.text: To match the age category of the faces, we selected 16 names commonly given in France to individuals born between 1995 and 2005 for the young adult faces, and 16 names commonly given to individuals born between 1945 and 1955 for the older adult faces.
Name selection was based on data from the Institut national de la statistique et des études économiques (INSEEfoot_0 ).
text.formatted: Name selection was based on data from the Institut national de la statistique et des études économiques (INSEE<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> ).

text.text: Each encoding trial began with a 300-ms fixation cross, followed by the presentation of a face and its associated name for 5 sec.
The complete set of face-name pairs was presented twice, with trial order randomized across participants, separately in each encoding block.
Following encoding, participants completed a 30-s distractor task in which they counted backward from 100.
They then performed a two-alternative forced-choice recognition test.
On each trial, a previously studied face was presented with two previously encountered names: the correct name and another name that was presented with a different face during the encoding phase.
Participants were asked to select the name that had previously been associated with the face by pressing the left or right arrow key.
They were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible.
The recognition test comprised 32 randomized trials.
The associations between faces and names were counterbalanced between participants such that the same face was not always associated with the same name.
For each participant, recognition accuracy was measured as the percentage of correct responses.

We used a face-name association task because this type of associative memory paradigm is known to engage the hippocampus (Macoir et al., 2024; Mayes et al., 2004; Polcher et al., 2017; Sperling et al., 2001).
text.formatted: We used a face-name association task because this type of associative memory paradigm is known to engage the hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Macoir et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Mayes et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Polcher et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Sperling et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The preprocessing pipeline was identical for object and scene tasks (and identical to the one previously used in Servais & Bastin, 2026).
text.formatted: The preprocessing pipeline was identical for object and scene tasks (and identical to the one previously used in <ref type="bibr">Servais & Bastin, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Gaze recordings were parsed into fixations and saccades using the event-detection algorithm provided by the SMI eye-tracking software.
Analyses were restricted to two predefined Areas of Interest (AOIs) corresponding to the left and right stimulus locations.
Each AOI covered a 300 × 300 px region, extended by a 25 px margin on all sides to accommodate possible gaze-estimation error.
Data quality was assessed at both the trial and participant levels.

A trial was retained when at least 50% of gaze samples were valid and when at least one of two additional criteria was satisfied: at least 30% of the valid samples were located within one of the AOIs, or cumulative gaze duration within the AOIs reached at least 500 ms.
Participants were included in the analyses if at least 75% of their gaze samples were valid overall and if they contributed a minimum of 15 valid trials, out of 30, in each experimental condition.
Eye-tracking measures were first extracted separately for the left and right AOIs and were then converted into indices of novelty preference.

In line with previous work examining gaze-based markers of novelty preference (Crutcher et al., 2009; Ernst et al., 2020; Leeman-Markowski et al., 2024), fixation-related measures included total fixation duration (ms), fixation count, and the location of the first fixation.
text.formatted: In line with previous work examining gaze-based markers of novelty preference <ref type="bibr">(Crutcher et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ernst et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Leeman-Markowski et al., 2024)</ref>, fixation-related measures included total fixation duration (ms), fixation count, and the location of the first fixation.

text.text: Saccade-related measures included the number of intra-AOI saccades, defined as saccades occurring within the same AOI.
For trials containing a novel and a familiar stimulus (Associative and Absolute conditions), noveltypreference indices were calculated as Novel/(Novel + Familiar) (Leeman-Markowski et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For trials containing a novel and a familiar stimulus (Associative and Absolute conditions), noveltypreference indices were calculated as Novel/(Novel + Familiar) <ref type="bibr">(Leeman-Markowski et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This transformation was applied to total fixation duration, fixation count, and intra-AOI saccade count.
First-fixation bias was additionally quantified as the proportion of valid trials on which the first fixation was directed toward the novel stimulus.
To control for participant-specific spatial preferences (Ković et al., 2009), novelty-preference measures were adjusted using performance on baseline trials.
text.formatted: To control for participant-specific spatial preferences <ref type="bibr">(Ković et al., 2009)</ref>, novelty-preference measures were adjusted using performance on baseline trials.

text.text: For each participant, a rightward attentional bias was estimated as the proportion of attention allocated to the right AOI relative to the total attention allocated to both AOIs, i.e., Right / (Left + Right).
This value was then expressed relative to the location of the novel stimulus on each trial.
When the novel stimulus was presented on the right, the rightward-bias value was retained; when it was presented on the left, its complement (1 -rightward bias) was used.
Baseline-corrected novelty preference was then calculated as Observed preference -Baseline bias.
Accordingly, a corrected score of zero reflected no novelty preference above and beyond the participant's spatial bias.
The same correction procedure was applied to all dependent measures, and all statistical analyses were performed on these baseline-adjusted scores.
Presence of novelty preference in older adults.
First, to verify that older adults show novelty preference for objects and scenes on the VPC tasks, we ran similar statistical models as those we used in Servais & Bastin (2026).
text.formatted: First, to verify that older adults show novelty preference for objects and scenes on the VPC tasks, we ran similar statistical models as those we used in <ref type="bibr">Servais & Bastin (2026)</ref>.

text.text: We ran trial-level mixed-effects models separately for the stimulus types and following dependent variables: baseline-corrected fixation time, fixation counts, and intra-AOI saccade counts.

To assess initial orienting, we analyzed whether the first fixation was directed to the novel image (1) or familiar image (0) using generalized linear mixed-effects models with a binomial distribution and logit link.
Details about the analyses and results are presented in Supplementary Materials (Supp.
in older adults.
To assess our main hypotheses regarding the relationship between memory performance and novelty processing, we conducted the preregistered correlations using Bayesian correlation analyses.
Novelty preference was quantified separately for Absolute novelty and Associative novelty, and separately for objects and scenes.

For each condition, novelty preference was indexed using baseline-corrected eye-tracking measures comprising the percentage of saccades directed toward the novel stimulus, the percentage of fixations directed toward the novel stimulus, fixation duration on the novel stimulus, and the proportion of trials in which the first fixation was directed toward the novel stimulus.

For Absolute novelty, we preregistered positive associations between novelty- For Associative novelty, we preregistered null associations between noveltypreference indices and performance on the DMS48, Doors Test, entity recognition task, oddone-out object task, FCSRT, and Face-Name associative memory task, for both object and scene novelty.
Correlations between Associative novelty preference and performance on the odd-one-out scene task were considered exploratory.
Bayes factors were used to quantify evidence for the preregistered hypotheses.
In accordance with the preregistration, BF10 > 3 was considered evidence in favor of a predicted positive association, whereas BF01 > 3 was considered evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.
text.formatted: In accordance with the preregistration, BF10 > 3 was considered evidence in favor of a predicted positive association, whereas BF01 > 3 was considered evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.

text.text: Bayes factors BF10 between 0.33 and 3 were interpreted as providing insufficient or only weak evidence to distinguish between the alternative and null hypotheses.

For correlations hypothesized to be positive, preregistered partial correlations controlling for TCI-R novelty-seeking scores were additionally conducted to determine whether the associations remained after accounting for individual differences in novelty-seeking traits.

To explore whether novelty preference changes in aging, we compared the novelty preference scores of our group of older adults with the scores from the group of younger adults (aged between 18-30 years old; N = 76 participants for the VPC object task; N = 77 participants for the VPC scene task) described in Servais & Bastin (2026) and available at DataVerse repository 2.
text.formatted: To explore whether novelty preference changes in aging, we compared the novelty preference scores of our group of older adults with the scores from the group of younger adults (aged between 18-30 years old; N = 76 participants for the VPC object task; N = 77 participants for the VPC scene task) described in <ref type="bibr">Servais & Bastin (2026)</ref> and available at DataVerse repository 2.

text.text: Analyses were conducted separately for the object and scene VPC tasks and for each eye-tracking novelty index (fixation time, fixation count, intra-AOI saccades, and firstfixation direction).

For the object task, age-related differences were assessed using a Bayesian 2 (Age Group: younger, older) × 2 (Novelty Condition: Absolute, Associative) mixed ANOVA, with Age Group as a between-participant factor and Novelty Condition as a within-participant factor.
For the scene task, an analogous Bayesian 2 (Age Group: younger, older) × 3 (Novelty Condition: Absolute, Associative, Incongruency) mixed ANOVA was performed.
For each analysis, Bayes factors were obtained through hierarchical model comparisons to assess the main effects of Age Group and Novelty Condition and their interaction.

BF10 quantified evidence in favor of the effect relative to its absence, whereas 2 https://doi.org/10.58119/ULG/QTNTHI BF01 , calculated as 1/BF10 , quantified evidence in favor of the absence of the effect.

text.text: The default "medium" prior scale was used for fixed effects (r = .50), with the nuisance prior specification used for the random participant effect.
Pupil data were processed in Python at the native sampling rate of 500 Hz and in their arbitrary unit.
Preprocessing was informed by the recommendations of Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023).
text.formatted: Preprocessing was informed by the recommendations of <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023)</ref>.

text.text: For each participant, the eye containing the greatest number of valid pupil samples was selected for analysis.
Samples with a pupil-confidence value below 1, according to the SMI software, were treated as missing.
Missing-data segments associated with invalid pupil samples were extended by 200 ms on either side to account for blink-related distortions.
Additional abrupt changes in pupil size were identified from the absolute rate of pupil-size change calculated using the actual sample timestamps.
Samples for which pupil-change speed exceeded the median speed by more than five median absolute deviations were marked as missing.
Short internal missingdata segments of up to 500 ms were reconstructed using cubic-spline interpolation.
Cubic splines were estimated using two valid samples preceding and two valid samples following the missing interval whenever these samples were available.
When sufficient surrounding samples were unavailable for cubic-spline estimation, linear interpolation was used as a fallback.
Missing segments longer than 500 ms and missing segments occurring at the edges of a recording were not interpolated.
Recordings were segmented into epochs extending from stimulus onset to 5 s after stimulus onset.

However, the time window of interest was defined as 1-4 s for stimulus onset in order to remove the early time window generally associated with light constriction during visual stimuli presentation and focus on the pupil response reflecting cognitive processing (Ferrari et al., 2016).
text.formatted: However, the time window of interest was defined as 1-4 s for stimulus onset in order to remove the early time window generally associated with light constriction during visual stimuli presentation and focus on the pupil response reflecting cognitive processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Ferrari et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The selected pupil signal was standardized within participant across the recording, resulting in pupil values expressed in participant-level z-score units.
Baseline pupil size was calculated from the final 500 ms of the immediately preceding SMI-labelled recording trial.
This strategy was used because the recording was interrupted between every trial, which did not allow us to use the signal just before stimulus onset.
The median pupil value within the cleaned baseline interval was then subtracted from the cleaned post-stimulus signal, yielding baseline-corrected pupil responses in participant-standardized units.
Trials were rejected when more than 20% of the raw pupil samples in the 0-5 s poststimulus interval were missing.
In addition, the baseline period was required to contain at least 80% valid cleaned samples.

Because the recording was interrupted between every trial due to a programming error, we have also discarded from the analyses all the trials that preceded breaks (11 trials per participant) as the interval between the end of the preceding baseline recording and stimulus onset exceeded 500 ms.
Participants for whom not at least one third of experimental trials passed the preprocessing criteria were excluded at this stage.
Pupil signal was smoothed using a centered median filter of approximately 100 ms.
Because the native sampling rate was 500 Hz, an odd 51-sample window was used, corresponding to approximately 102 ms, in order to define the filter symmetrically around each sample.
The filtered signal was subsequently downsampled from 500 Hz to 100 Hz.
A regular 100-Hz analysis time grid was then assigned to the resulting signal, corresponding to one pupil observation every 10 ms.
The original acquisition-relative timestamps were retained separately for quality-control purposes.
Preregistered pupil measures were calculated from the baseline-corrected signal between 1 and 4 s after stimulus onset, thereby minimizing the contribution of the initial light-evoked pupil response.
Peak constriction and dilation were defined as the minimum and maximum pupil responses, respectively, within this interval.

Following an approach adapted from Kafkas and Montaldi (2015), peak amplitude was estimated as the mean of the three samples immediately preceding and three samples immediately following the identified extremum.
text.formatted: Following an approach adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kafkas and Montaldi (2015)</ref>, peak amplitude was estimated as the mean of the three samples immediately preceding and three samples immediately following the identified extremum.

text.text: Mean pupil response and signed area under the curve (AUC) were calculated over the same 1-4 s interval.
Differences in pupil response across conditions were examined using linear mixed-effects models.
Separate models were fitted for peak dilation, peak constriction, mean pupil response, and AUC.
Condition (Absolute novelty, Associative novelty, and Familiar) was entered as a categorical fixed effect, with the Familiar condition specified as the reference category.

The resulting fixed-effect contrasts therefore tested whether each pupil-response measure differed between the Absolute novelty and Familiar conditions and between the Associative novelty and Familiar conditions.
To account for stimulus-level visual characteristics that could influence pupil responses, image saliency, visual complexity, and aesthetic value were included as fixedeffect covariates.
Image complexity was quantified using edge count, a computational measure of visual complexity that has been shown to correlate with human complexity judgments (Machado et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Image complexity was quantified using edge count, a computational measure of visual complexity that has been shown to correlate with human complexity judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Machado et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Image saliency was quantified as mean saliency using SaliencyToolbox 2.3 (Walther & Koch, 2006), and aesthetic value was represented by mean aesthetic ratings obtained from an independent normative study (Servais & Bastin, 2026).
text.formatted: Image saliency was quantified as mean saliency using SaliencyToolbox 2.3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Walther & Koch, 2006)</ref>, and aesthetic value was represented by mean aesthetic ratings obtained from an independent normative study <ref type="bibr">(Servais & Bastin, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: All stimulus-level covariates were standardized prior to analysis.

To account for the crossed participant-by-stimulus structure of the data, the initial random-effects specification included random intercepts for participant and stimulus, together with participant-specific random slopes for both condition contrasts (Associative novelty versus Familiar and Absolute novelty versus Familiar).
Models were estimated by maximum likelihood using the MixedLM implementation in statsmodels with Powell optimization.

When the estimated variance of a random slope collapsed to, or effectively approached, zero, indicating a boundary solution and lack of support for that variance component, the corresponding random slope was removed and the model was refitted.
Random-effects simplification was performed sequentially while leaving the fixed-effects specification unchanged.
Preregistered correlations between pupil responses and memory performance in older adults.
For the preregistered pupil-memory analyses, trial-level pupil measures were first averaged within participant and condition.
Three indices were considered for each type of novelty: peak response, mean response, and signed area under the curve (AUC), all calculated over the 1-4 s post-stimulus interval.
To isolate novelty-specific pupil responses, each measure was expressed relative to the Familiar condition.
Absolute-novelty indices were calculated as Familiar minus Absolute, such that larger positive values represented stronger Absolute-specific constriction.
Associative-novelty indices were calculated as Associative minus Familiar, such that larger positive values represented stronger Associative-specific dilation.

To assess our hypotheses regarding the relationship between memory performance and novelty-related pupil responses, we conducted preregistered Bayesian correlation analyses between pupil novelty responses and memory performance on the same test battery as for the VPC-like tasks.

We preregistered positive associations between pupil responses to Absolute novelty (mean response, AUC, and peak constriction) and performance on the DMS48 test, Doors test, entity recognition task, and odd-one-out object task.
Thus, individuals showing stronger pupil responses to Absolute novelty were expected to show better performance on these memory measures.
In contrast, no association was expected between pupil response to Absolute novelty and performance on the FCSRT/RLRI16 or Face-Name associative memory task.
For pupil responses to Associative novelty (mean, AUC, and peak dilation), we predicted null associations to all abovementioned memory tasks.
Bayes factors were used to quantify evidence for the preregistered hypotheses.

For predicted positive associations, BF10 > 3 together with a positive correlation coefficient was considered evidence in favor of the preregistered hypothesis, whereas BF01 > 3 was considered evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.
text.formatted: For predicted positive associations, BF10 > 3 together with a positive correlation coefficient was considered evidence in favor of the preregistered hypothesis, whereas BF01 > 3 was considered evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.

text.text: Bayes factors between 0.33 and 3 were interpreted as providing insufficient evidence to distinguish between the alternative and null hypotheses.
In addition to the preregistered peak-response analyses, we conducted exploratory analyses of the complementary peak response for each novelty type.
Specifically, we examined peak dilation for Absolute novelty and peak constriction for Associative novelty.
Because these analyses were exploratory, evidence was quantified using two-sided BF10 values rather than the preregistered hypothesis-specific evidence classification.
