The present study primarily examined whether eye-movement behavior and pupil responses to different forms of novelty, considered as behavioral and physiological indices of novelty processing, were associated with individual differences in memory performance across a range of tasks in older adults.
Importantly, we distinguished between Absolute and Associative novelty, as well as between object-and scene-based processing.

We hypothesized that Absolute novelty processing, which is assumed to depend on PRC integrity (Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018), particularly for objects, could be associated with performance on familiarity-based recognition tasks or perceptual discrimination tasks, known to involve the PRC (Bastin & Delhaye, 2023; Martin & Barense, 2023).
text.formatted: We hypothesized that Absolute novelty processing, which is assumed to depend on PRC integrity <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018)</ref>, particularly for objects, could be associated with performance on familiarity-based recognition tasks or perceptual discrimination tasks, known to involve the PRC <ref type="bibr">(Bastin & Delhaye, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Martin & Barense, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, we expected Associative novelty processing to be relatively independent of episodic memory performance, including free recall and cross-domain associative memory.

Although both Associative novelty processing and episodic memory have been linked to the hippocampus integrity (Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018), they may rely on partly distinct hippocampal mechanisms (Barbeau et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Although both Associative novelty processing and episodic memory have been linked to the hippocampus integrity <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018)</ref>, they may rely on partly distinct hippocampal mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barbeau et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, shared reliance on the hippocampus does not necessarily imply that individual differences in Associative novelty responses should covary with episodic memory performance.

Accordingly, our primary analyses used Bayesian correlations to examine the relationships between performance across the memory tasks and eye-tracking and pupillary responses to both Absolute and Associative novelty.
Before considering these individual-difference associations, it is important to establish that the VPC-like tasks elicited reliable novelty responses at the group level.
Older adults showed robust novelty preferences on the VPC-like tasks.

For both objects and scenes, participants preferentially attended to Absolute and Associative novel stimuli across eyetracking measures (fixation time, fixation count, intra-AOI saccades, and first-fixation direction).
In contrast, the Incongruency manipulation (i.e., objects that were congruent versus incongruent with the surrounding scene) did not elicit reliable novelty preference.

As the procedure was the same as that used with younger adults aged 18-30 years from a prior study (Servais & Bastin, 2026), we conducted exploratory analyses to compare novelty preference patterns across age groups.
text.formatted: As the procedure was the same as that used with younger adults aged 18-30 years from a prior study <ref type="bibr">(Servais & Bastin, 2026)</ref>, we conducted exploratory analyses to compare novelty preference patterns across age groups.

text.text: These additional Bayesian analyses suggested that novelty-preference patterns were largely comparable between younger and older adults.
Importantly, however, the presence of robust novelty preferences at the group level did not translate into the predicted relationships with individual differences in memory performance.

The preregistered prediction that stronger responses to Absolute novelty would be associated with better performance on familiarity-based recognition or PRC-dependent perceptual discrimination tasks received no support.

Instead, most correlations between Absolute novelty-preference measures from the VPC-like task for object and memory performance provided evidence in favor of the absence of an association, or remained inconclusive.
A similar pattern emerged for scenes, for which correlations involving Absolute novelty preference predominantly supported the null hypothesis.
Regarding Associative novelty preference, the overall pattern largely supported the preregistered null hypotheses.
For scenes, most associations provided evidence for the absence of a relationship, and none provided evidence for an association with memory performance.
For objects, however, although most associations predicted to be null were supported as null by the Bayesian analyses, a few departures from the null involved FCSRT performance.

Greater novelty preference in terms of saccade count was associated with better Free Recall, whereas greater fixation-count and first-fixation preferences were associated with poorer Total Recall or ISC performance.

Because these effects differed both in the eyetracking measure involved, and in their direction, they do not suggest a straightforward relationship whereby stronger Associative novelty processing is associated with better episodic memory.

Importantly, their absence in the VPC-like task with scenes further suggests that these associations may be specific to the way Associative novelty was instantiated or explored in the object task, rather than reflecting a general relationship between Associative novelty processing and memory ability.

Given that FCSRT performance has been associated with hippocampal functioning (Sarazin et al., 2010 , Zammit et al., 2017), one possibility is that some forms of prolonged attention toward associatively novel objects reflect greater processing demands or unresolved prediction error rather than more efficient novelty processing (Kumaran & Maguire, 2007; Wills et al., 2007).

text.text: In this view, the negative associations with Total Recall and ISC could indicate that Associative novelty processing is more effortful in individuals with lower episodic-memory performance.

This interpretation may be particularly relevant for the object task, in which Associative novelty was instantiated using chimeric objects that may impose greater perceptual or integrative processing demands (Magnié et al., 2003).
text.formatted: This interpretation may be particularly relevant for the object task, in which Associative novelty was instantiated using chimeric objects that may impose greater perceptual or integrative processing demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Magnié et al., 2003)</ref>.

Associative novelty compared to Absolute novelty (Servais & Bastin, 2026).
text.formatted: Associative novelty compared to Absolute novelty <ref type="bibr">(Servais & Bastin, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, this account remains speculative, particularly because greater saccade-based novelty preference was positively associated with Free Recall.
Moreover, the FCSRT provides partly distinct measures of episodic-memory performance.

Free Recall primarily reflects spontaneous retrieval, whereas Total Recall and the ISC quantify the extent to which retrieval benefits from semantic cues (Grober et al., 2010; Quenon et al., 2016; Bussè et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Free Recall primarily reflects spontaneous retrieval, whereas Total Recall and the ISC quantify the extent to which retrieval benefits from semantic cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Grober et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Quenon et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Bussè et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The opposing associations may therefore reflect relationships between distinct components of novelty-directed exploration and memory, rather than a single, uniform association between Associative novelty processing and episodic-memory ability.
More broadly, novelty processing itself is supported by a distributed network encompassing sensory cortices, MTL structures, as well as frontal salience and control regions (Wong et al., 2026).
text.formatted: More broadly, novelty processing itself is supported by a distributed network encompassing sensory cortices, MTL structures, as well as frontal salience and control regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Wong et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Because performance on a complex episodic-memory task such as the FCSRT likewise depends on multiple cognitive operations, the isolated associations observed here may arise from partially shared processes rather than from a direct correspondence between hippocampal Associativenovelty processing and episodic-memory capacity.
However, given the small number of effects and their heterogeneous directions, these possible interpretations remain tentative and require replication.

Future studies combining eye tracking with electrophysiological measures such as EEG could help clarify the underlying mechanisms by disentangling attentional, prediction-error, and memory-related processes across the temporal cascade of novelty processing for both Absolute and Associative novelty.
The pupil findings provided a complementary, but different, perspective.
At the group level, neither Absolute nor Associative novelty differed reliably from the Familiar condition for peak constriction, mean pupil response, AUC, or peak dilation.

This pattern remained unchanged after accounting for stimulus-level characteristics such as saliency, visual complexity, and aesthetic value, and was similarly observed when younger and older adults were examined separately (see Supp.
Thus, unlike the clear novelty effects observed in overt viewing behavior on VPC-like tasks, novelty was not accompanied by a robust average change in the pupil measures.
This distinction suggests that spontaneous orienting toward novelty and pupil responses to novelty need not provide interchangeable measures of novelty processing.
When compared with younger adults, there was no compelling evidence for age-group differences in peak constriction, mean pupil response, or AUC.

In contrast, peak dilation showed evidence for an age-group difference, with younger adults exhibiting more positive Familiar-corrected dilation than older adults for both Absolute and Associative novelty.

The absence of an Age Group × Novelty Condition interaction indicates that this difference was not specific to either type of novelty, but instead reflected a more general age-related difference in pupillary responsiveness.

This reduced peak dilation in older adults may partly reflect normative age-related changes in pupillary physiology, as ageing is associated with a reduced pupillary dynamic range and attenuated dilation responses (Bitsios et al., 1996; Riley et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This reduced peak dilation in older adults may partly reflect normative age-related changes in pupillary physiology, as ageing is associated with a reduced pupillary dynamic range and attenuated dilation responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bitsios et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Riley et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond these peripheral physiological changes, task-evoked pupil dilation has also been linked to activity of the locus coeruleus-noradrenergic system (Murphy et al., 2014), which itself undergoes age-related changes (Shibata et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Beyond these peripheral physiological changes, task-evoked pupil dilation has also been linked to activity of the locus coeruleus-noradrenergic system <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Murphy et al., 2014)</ref>, which itself undergoes age-related changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Shibata et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: However, because pupil dilation is not a specific measure of LC activity, this interpretation remains tentative and would require direct assessment of LC integrity to be confirmed.
The analysis of correlations between novelty-related pupil responses to novel (Absolute or Associative) objects and performance on memory tasks showed a pattern broadly consistent with the VPC one.

Most of the preregistered positive associations between Absolute novelty indices and the DMS48, Doors, entity recognition, and odd-one-out object measures favored the null, and the remaining two were inconclusive.
For Absolute novelty, most preregistered null associations were also supported as null.

One notable exception was the positive relationship between greater Absolute novelty-related peak constriction and FCSRT Total Recall, which provided strong evidence against the predicted null hypothesis.
Although this association with FCSRT Total Recall was not predicted, it may point to processes shared between the pupillary response to Absolute novelty and episodic-memory functioning.

Absolute novelty has previously been associated with reduced pupil dilation or greater constriction, which has been proposed to reflect parasympathetic and cholinergic mechanisms involved in prioritizing and encoding novel information (Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018).
text.formatted: Absolute novelty has previously been associated with reduced pupil dilation or greater constriction, which has been proposed to reflect parasympathetic and cholinergic mechanisms involved in prioritizing and encoding novel information <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kafkas & Montaldi, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Given that FCSRT Total Recall has also been related to hippocampal integrity (Sarazin et al., 2010), individuals showing a stronger constrictive response to Absolute novelty may also possess more efficient neural mechanisms supporting episodic-memory processing.
text.formatted: Given that FCSRT Total Recall has also been related to hippocampal integrity <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Sarazin et al., 2010)</ref>, individuals showing a stronger constrictive response to Absolute novelty may also possess more efficient neural mechanisms supporting episodic-memory processing.

text.text: This hypothetical interpretation differs from our preregistered hypothesis linking Absolute novelty specifically to perirhinal functioning, and may instead suggest that the peak-constriction response captures a broader novelty-related encoding mechanism.
Nevertheless, this finding was relatively isolated.
The corresponding association with FCSRT ISC remained inconclusive, and the effect did not generalize across the other pupil indices.

Similarly, for Associative novelty, the large majority of confirmatory correlations supported the preregistered null hypothesis, except the correlations of peak dilation with FCSRT Free Recall and ISC, which remained inconclusive.
Consequently, the association between Absolute novelty-related peak constriction and FCSRT Total Recall should be considered preliminary and requires further investigation.

The convergence between the novelty-related behavior on the VPC-like tasks and pupil responses correlation analyses is noteworthy, but should be interpreted in light of the different strength of the underlying novelty effects.
For the VPC-like tasks, older adults showed robust group-level novelty preferences, yet these individual differences were largely unrelated to memory performance.
This provides relatively strong evidence that spontaneous novelty preferences in viewing behavior are not entirely dependent on episodic memory abilities.

The pupil findings pointed in the same general direction, but are more difficult to interpret because neither Absolute nor Associative novelty produced reliable group-level differences from the Familiar condition, even in younger adults.
Consequently, Familiarcorrected individual-difference indices may have contained relatively more measurement noise, potentially limiting their ability to reveal associations with memory performance.
In VPC-like tasks, the dissociation between robust group-level novelty responses and weak individual-level associations with memory performance is theoretically informative.

Previous demonstrations of relationships between novelty processing and memory may partly depend on paradigms in which novelty detection itself requires recognition of, or comparison with, previously encountered information.
By using novelty paradigms in which memory confound was minimized, the present study may provide a more selective assessment of spontaneous novelty processing and orienting.
From this perspective, novelty processing may be more functionally separable from episodic-related memory abilities than initially hypothesized.
An important next step will be to characterize more precisely the neural substrates underlying Absolute and Associative novelty, as operationalized in the present paradigms.

A small number of fMRI studies have investigated forms of novelty broadly corresponding to our definitions of either Absolute novelty, using unfamiliar non-objects (Harı & Demiralp, 2025), rare or uncommon objects (Blackford et al., 2010), or abstract fractals (Stoppel et al., 2009), or Associative novelty using familiar objects with unusual features (Michelon et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013).
text.formatted: A small number of fMRI studies have investigated forms of novelty broadly corresponding to our definitions of either Absolute novelty, using unfamiliar non-objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Harı & Demiralp, 2025)</ref>, rare or uncommon objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Blackford et al., 2010)</ref>, or abstract fractals <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Stoppel et al., 2009)</ref>, or Associative novelty using familiar objects with unusual features <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Michelon et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Wang et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Zhang et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Like the present study, these investigations assessed novelty without relying on an explicit familiarization phase, allowing novelty to be defined in relation to pre-existing knowledge rather than recent episodic exposure, thereby reducing potential confounds with episodic recognition processes.

Interestingly, these neuroimaging studies have implicated not only MTL structures but also the fusiform and occipital gyri (Harı & Demiralp, 2025), inferior frontal gyrus, anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus (Blackford et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Interestingly, these neuroimaging studies have implicated not only MTL structures but also the fusiform and occipital gyri <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Harı & Demiralp, 2025)</ref>, inferior frontal gyrus, anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Blackford et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Zhang et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These findings raise the possibility that novelty detection recruits a distributed neural network extending beyond regions traditionally associated with episodic memory, potentially accounting for the relative independence between novelty preference and episodic memory abilities observed in the present study.

Future studies combining whole-brain analyses with high-resolution fMRI to directly compare Absolute and Associative novelty across objects and scenes would therefore be particularly valuable for determining the extent to which these forms of novelty recruit shared or distinct neural networks, and how these networks relate to those supporting episodic memory.

From an aging perspective, the preserved VPC-like novelty-preference patterns are potentially encouraging, as they suggest that the ability to detect and orient toward novel information can remain relatively intact despite variability in episodic memory performance.
Whether the same conclusion extends to pupillary novelty responses remains less certain and will require paradigms that elicit more reliable novelty-related pupil effects.
A key direction for future research would be to investigate whether similar patterns are observed in clinical populations characterized by brain damage to the MTL and episodic memory impairment.
Such populations could provide a particularly informative test of the extent to which different forms of novelty processing depend on the integrity of the episodic memory system.

This question is particularly relevant given the growing interest in traditional VPC paradigms as potential markers of cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease (Crutcher et al., 2009; Boujelbane et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This question is particularly relevant given the growing interest in traditional VPC paradigms as potential markers of cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease <ref type="bibr">(Crutcher et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Boujelbane et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, however, traditional VPC tasks intrinsically incorporate a recognition-memory component: participants must retain information from a familiarization phase in order to distinguish previously viewed from novel stimuli at test.

Indeed, Crutcher et al. (2009) found that individuals with mild cognitive impairment showed novelty preferences comparable to controls at a very short retention interval, whereas their novelty preference was reduced when the delay was extended to two minutes.
text.formatted: Indeed, <ref type="bibr">Crutcher et al. (2009)</ref> found that individuals with mild cognitive impairment showed novelty preferences comparable to controls at a very short retention interval, whereas their novelty preference was reduced when the delay was extended to two minutes.

text.text: Thus, reduced novelty preference may, at least partly, reflect difficulty maintaining or retrieving the familiar representation rather than a primary impairment in novelty detection itself.

This distinction may also help reconcile the present findings with previous reports of age-related reductions in novelty preference obtained with paradigms containing stronger associative-memory demands (e.g., Allegretti et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This distinction may also help reconcile the present findings with previous reports of age-related reductions in novelty preference obtained with paradigms containing stronger associative-memory demands (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Allegretti et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In this regard, our paradigm provides a novel approach by reducing recognition and retention demands and focusing more directly on spontaneous responses to different forms of novelty.

Applying these tasks to individuals with MCI, Alzheimer's disease or MTL amnesia would help determine whether novelty processing itself becomes impaired with medial temporal pathology, independently of the memory demands inherent in traditional VPC procedures (Basile et al., 2024; Eizenman et al., 2019; Leeman-Markowski et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Applying these tasks to individuals with MCI, Alzheimer's disease or MTL amnesia would help determine whether novelty processing itself becomes impaired with medial temporal pathology, independently of the memory demands inherent in traditional VPC procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Basile et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Eizenman et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Leeman-Markowski et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such work could also test whether Absolute and Associative novelty show different trajectories of vulnerability.
Finally, the relative resistance of VPC-like novelty preferences to healthy aging may be advantageous from a clinical perspective.

If future studies demonstrate that these responses remain stable during normative aging but become selectively disrupted by neurodegenerative pathology, they could potentially help distinguish disease-related changes from the effects of age itself with good specificity.
We would like to draw attention to a couple of limitations that should be considered when interpreting the present findings.
First, the memory tasks used here cannot be regarded as process-pure measures of perirhinal-or hippocampal-dependent functioning.

Although our hypotheses were based on evidence linking particular tasks or memory processes preferentially to one MTL structure, the PRC and hippocampus operate within highly interconnected systems, and tasks intended to engage one region frequently recruit the other as well (Besson et al., 2020; Shrager et al., 2008; Staresina et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Although our hypotheses were based on evidence linking particular tasks or memory processes preferentially to one MTL structure, the PRC and hippocampus operate within highly interconnected systems, and tasks intended to engage one region frequently recruit the other as well <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Besson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Shrager et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Staresina et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the variability in memory performance within our healthy older-adult sample is relatively restricted for some of the tests.
Participants were generally cognitively high functioning, with a mean MoCA score of 27.68, and several memory measures approached their maximum possible scores.
For example, mean performance was 45.27 out of 48 on the DMS48 and 46.17 out of 48 for FCSRT Total Recall.

Such restricted between-participant variability may attenuate correlations and reduce the ability to detect meaningful individual differences in the relationship between novelty responses and memory performance.
Future studies including individuals with a broader range of cognitive and MTL functioning, including clinical populations as mentioned above, may provide a stronger test of these relationships.

Across stimulus versions, inter-rater reliability was generally good for the three rating dimensions, as indexed by one-way average-measures intraclass correlation coefficients, ICC(1,k).
For novelty ratings, ICC values ranged from .70 to .86, indicating moderate-togood agreement among raters regarding the mean novelty of the object images.
Similar levels of reliability were observed for surprise ratings, with ICC values ranging from .77 to .85.
Reliability for bizarreness ratings was somewhat more variable, with ICC values ranging from .58 to .83.
Although most versions showed good agreement for bizarreness, the lower ICC observed in V4 suggests that this dimension may have been interpreted less consistently in that version.

Overall, these results indicate that aggregated ratings were reliable across versions, particularly for novelty and surprise, while bizarreness showed slightly greater variability in inter-rater agreement.

text.text: Analyses.

For the scenes VPC task, trial-level data were analyzed using mixed-effects models analogous to those used for the objects task, but Condition had three levels-Absolute novelty, Associative novelty, and Incongruency.
The Condition was coded without an intercept, so each coefficient estimated condition-specific novelty preference and tested whether it differed from zero.
Pairwise contrasts compared all conditions, with p-values adjusted using the Holm correction (Holm, 1979).

Initial orienting was analyzed using generalized linear mixed-effects models with a binomial distribution and logit link, as in the objects task.
Condition again had three levels and was coded without an intercept.
Condition-specific coefficients tested deviation from chance, and pairwise contrasts assessed whether initial fixation orienting differed across novelty types.

Normative ratings of older adults for the (in)congruent object-in-scene images from the VPC task for scenes.

To collect normative ratings for the congruent and incongruent object-in-scene images in older adults, we ran an online experiment using Gorilla to collect subjective ratings of 39 participants (22 females) aged above 55 years old (66.3 years on average, SD = 4.84).
Participants were recruited via Prolifics.
In the first part of that experiment (Supp.

Fig. 1A), participants rated their subjective. experience of novelty, surprise, and bizarreness for congruent or incongruent object-in-scene images according to the same definitions as provided in the main normative study described earlier and using continuous slider scales ranging from 0 to 100.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure">1A</ref>), participants rated their subjective. experience of novelty, surprise, and bizarreness for congruent or incongruent object-in-scene images according to the same definitions as provided in the main normative study described earlier and using continuous slider scales ranging from 0 to 100.

text.text: In this experiment, we also asked participants to provide the same ratings for scene images from the Absolute (30 images) and Associative (30 images) novelty conditions so that we could directly compare these different conditions in terms of novelty intensity.
In the second part of the experiment (Supp.
Fig. 1C), participants were presented with pairs of images: one showing an object and the other showing a scene.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure">1C</ref>), participants were presented with pairs of images: one showing an object and the other showing a scene.

text.text: For each trial, both images were displayed simultaneously, and participants were asked to judge how likely it is for the object to appear in the given room.
Their response was recorded using a continuous slider ranging from 0 (not likely at all) to 100 (very likely) allowing for nuanced assessments of perceived fit between object and context.
Trials were randomized according to experimental conditions (congruent vs. incongruent pairings) to ensure variability in presentation order.
To prevent participants from seeing both versions of the same stimulus, four different versions of the task were created, each containing distinct subsets of stimuli.
Participants completed both part 1 and part 2 using different subsets, ensuring no overlap in stimuli across parts.

text.text: Controlling for novelty seeking did not materially alter the pattern of results.
None of the 40 preregistered positive associations provided evidence for the predicted positive relationship after adjustment for TCI-R scores.
For object novelty, 12 of the 20 partial correlations provided evidence favoring the null hypothesis (BF10 < 0.33), whereas eight were inconclusive (BF10 = 0.33-3).

text.text: For scene novelty, 18 of the 20 partial correlations provided evidence favoring the null and two were inconclusive.

Relative to the zero-order analyses, four associations shifted from evidence favoring the null to inconclusive evidence: first-fixation preference for novel objects with DMS48 performance, partial r = -.18, BF10 = 0.40, and entity-recognition performance, partial r = -.18, BF10 = 0.39; and the percentage of fixations and fixation duration directed toward novel scenes with Doors A performance, partial rs = -.19 and -.19, BF10 s = 0.45 and 0.49, respectively.
Importantly, these changes reflected slightly stronger negative rather than positive associations.
Overall, controlling for novelty-seeking traits therefore did not reveal evidence for the preregistered positive relationships between Absolute novelty preference and memory performance.
